meta.description: Developmental milestone checklists used by the rules engine (backend/rules.py) to screen for possible red flags. This is a screening aid only, never a diagnosis.
meta.coverage: Ages 2 months through 5 years are sourced from the CDC 'Learn the Signs. Act Early.' (LTSAE) milestone checklists, fetched 2026-10-18. Domains follow CDC's own categories: Social/Emotional, Language/Communication, Cognitive, Movement/Physical Development.

not_yet_covered.vision_hearing: Researched 2026-10-18 (deeper pass): found real, specific primary sources, but none usable verbatim here due to copyright or format: (1) Hearing — state Early Hearing Detection & Intervention (EHDI) programs (e.g. Indiana's, at secure.in.gov) publish a 0-24-month parent-facing hearing/language milestone checklist; no explicit copyright/rights-reserved notice was found on the specific document fetched, but it is state-authored material, not U.S. federal public domain like CDC's LTSAE, so its exact wording was NOT copied here. (2) Vision — Prevent Blindness's National Center for Children's Vision and Eye Health publishes '18 Key Vision Developmental Milestones From Birth to Baby's First Birthday' (nationalcenter.preventblindness.org), a real, well-credentialed, expert-reviewed checklist (contributors include a Johns Hopkins pediatric ophthalmologist) — but it is explicitly marked '©2020 Prevent Blindness. All rights reserved,' so per the copyright-caution rule its item text was NOT copied here either. AAP/AAPOS vision guidance (Donahue et al. 2016, Pediatrics) covers in-clinic screening ages/instruments, not a parent-reportable checklist. Next step: either (a) request written permission from Prevent Blindness (contact: nottingham@preventblindness.org) to adapt their 18-milestone tool, and separately confirm the EHDI material's reuse terms with the issuing state/NCHAM, or (b) have a pediatric/audiology/ophthalmology reviewer author original milestone wording from the underlying clinical facts (facts aren't copyrightable, only this specific expression of them), citing these sources as background. Do not add entries here until one of those happens.
not_yet_covered.growth: Sourced 2026-10-18: official CDC and WHO growth chart LMS/percentile data files, downloaded verbatim into data/growth/ (see data/growth/README.md) from cdc.gov/growthcharts. These are percentile-curve data, not a milestone checklist, so they live in their own files/format rather than as entries in this JSON.
not_yet_covered.school_age_adolescent_behavior: Researched 2026-10-18 (deeper pass, fetched primary sources directly): (1) PHQ-A — CONFIRMED public domain. The official PHQ instruction manual (phqscreeners.com) states verbatim: 'All of the measures included in Table 1 are in the public domain. No permission is required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute,' and Table 1 explicitly lists PHQ-A. However, this manual does NOT itself contain the PHQ-A's items — its own text says the PHQ-A's 'diagnostic scoring [is] described in manual, available upon request.' So the license is confirmed, but the actual item text still needs to be requested from phqscreeners.com before it can be added here. (2) PSC-17 — a full 35-item Pediatric Symptom Checklist (parent PSC and youth Y-PSC), with item text, cutoff scores, and scoring instructions, was found in an official Bright Futures (AAP/HRSA) 'Tool for Professionals' PDF (brightfutures.org) citing Jellinek & Murphy (Massachusetts General Hospital) as developers; no explicit copyright/rights-reserved restriction was visible in that document. This is the 35-item PSC, not the PSC-17 short form specifically — the exact 17-item subset and its 3 subscales (attention/internalizing/externalizing) must be confirmed against the original validation paper (Gardner et al. 1999) before using a subset, since using the wrong items invalidates the measure. It was NOT added here pending that confirmation and a direct license check with psc.partners.org / MGH. (3) Vanderbilt — the NICHQ 1st edition (2002) is explicitly free to download with a request to cite NICHQ; however, forms from the 2nd/3rd editions circulating online carry an AAP 'Copyright © 2012 American Academy of Pediatrics. All Rights Reserved' notice, so edition matters. Use only the 1st edition content (with citation) or obtain explicit AAP/NICHQ permission for later editions. None of these three instruments' item text was added to this file this pass. Before integrating any of them: get written confirmation of current terms from the primary source, resolve the PSC-17 subset question, then add as a separate, properly licensed questionnaire module (not milestone entries), with pediatric/clinical sign-off.

cdc_ltsae.name: CDC "Learn the Signs. Act Early." (LTSAE) developmental milestone checklists
cdc_ltsae.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
cdc_ltsae.license_note: U.S. federal government public health material. Verify current version/terms at cdc.gov before relying on it in production.
cdc_ltsae.disclaimer: CDC states these checklists are not a substitute for standardized, validated developmental screening tools (e.g. ASQ-3, M-CHAT-R/F).

general_guidance.when_to_act: If a child is not meeting one or more milestones for their age, has lost a skill they once had (regression), or a parent has any other concern, CDC's guidance is to act early: talk with the child's doctor and ask about formal developmental screening, rather than waiting.
general_guidance.corrected_age_note: For children born before 37 weeks, CDC/AAP guidance (reflected in Agents.md Hard rules) is to use corrected age, not chronological age, when checking milestones until the child is 2 years old.
general_guidance.next_steps: If concerns remain after talking with the doctor, ask for a referral to a specialist, and contact the family's state/territory early intervention program (CDC maintains a directory at cdc.gov/FindEI).

social_emotional.text: Calms down when spoken to or picked up
Looks at your face
Seems happy to see you when you walk up to her
Smiles when you talk to or smile at her

language_communication.text: Makes sounds other than crying
Reacts to loud sounds

cognitive.text: Watches you as you move
Looks at a toy for several seconds

movement_physical.text: Holds head up when on tummy
Moves both arms and both legs
Opens hands briefly

social_emotional.text: Smiles on his own to get your attention
Chuckles (not yet a full laugh) when you try to make him laugh
Looks at you, moves, or makes sounds to get or keep your attention

language_communication.text: Makes sounds like "oooo", "aahh" (cooing)
Makes sounds back when you talk to him
Turns head towards the sound of your voice

cognitive.text: If hungry, opens mouth when he sees breast or bottle
Looks at her hands with interest

movement_physical.text: Holds head steady without support when you are holding him
Holds a toy when you put it in his hand
Uses his arm to swing at toys
Brings hands to mouth
Pushes up onto elbows/forearms when on tummy

social_emotional.text: Knows familiar people
Likes to look at self in a mirror
Laughs

language_communication.text: Takes turns making sounds with you
Blows "raspberries" (sticks tongue out and blows)
Makes squealing noises

cognitive.text: Puts things in her mouth to explore them
Reaches to grab a toy she wants
Closes lips to show she doesn't want more food

movement_physical.text: Rolls from tummy to back
Pushes up with straight arms when on tummy
Leans on hands to support herself when sitting

social_emotional.text: Is shy, clingy, or fearful around strangers
Shows several facial expressions, like happy, sad, angry, and surprised
Looks when you call her name
Reacts when you leave (looks, reaches for you, or cries)
Smiles or laughs when you play peek-a-boo

language_communication.text: Makes a lot of different sounds like "mamamama" and "bababababa"
Lifts arms up to be picked up

cognitive.text: Looks for objects when dropped out of sight (like his spoon or toy)
Bangs two things together

movement_physical.text: Gets to a sitting position by herself
Moves things from one hand to her other hand
Uses fingers to "rake" food towards himself
Sits without support

social_emotional.text: Plays games with you, like pat-a-cake

language_communication.text: Waves "bye-bye"
Calls a parent "mama" or "dada" or another special name
Understands "no" (pauses briefly or stops when you say it)

cognitive.text: Puts something in a container, like a block in a cup
Looks for things he sees you hide, like a toy under a blanket

movement_physical.text: Pulls up to stand
Walks, holding on to furniture
Drinks from a cup without a lid, as you hold it
Picks things up between thumb and pointer finger, like small bits of food

social_emotional.text: Copies other children while playing, like taking toys out of a container when another child does
Shows you an object she likes
Claps when excited
Hugs stuffed doll or other toy
Shows you affection (hugs, cuddles, or kisses you)

language_communication.text: Tries to say one or two words besides "mama" or "dada," like "ba" for ball or "da" for dog
Looks at a familiar object when you name it
Follows directions given with both a gesture and words (e.g. hands over a toy when told "Give me the toy")
Points to ask for something or to get help

cognitive.text: Tries to use things the right way, like a phone, cup, or book
Stacks at least two small objects, like blocks

movement_physical.text: Takes a few steps on his own
Uses fingers to feed herself some food

social_emotional.text: Moves away from you, but looks to make sure you are close by
Points to show you something interesting
Puts hands out for you to wash them
Looks at a few pages in a book with you
Helps you dress him by pushing arm through sleeve or lifting up foot

language_communication.text: Tries to say three or more words besides "mama" or "dada"
Follows one-step directions without any gestures, like giving you the toy when you say, "Give it to me."

cognitive.text: Copies you doing chores, like sweeping with a broom
Plays with toys in a simple way, like pushing a toy car

movement_physical.text: Walks without holding on to anyone or anything
Scribbles
Drinks from a cup without a lid and may spill sometimes
Feeds himself with his fingers
Tries to use a spoon
Climbs on and off a couch or chair without help

social_emotional.text: Notices when others are hurt or upset, like pausing or looking sad when someone is crying
Looks at your face to see how to react in a new situation

language_communication.text: Points to things in a book when you ask, like "Where is the bear?"
Says at least two words together, like "More milk."
Points to at least two body parts when you ask him to show you
Uses more gestures than just waving and pointing, like blowing a kiss or nodding yes

cognitive.text: Holds something in one hand while using the other hand; for example, holding a container and taking the lid off
Tries to use switches, knobs, or buttons on a toy
Plays with more than one toy at the same time, like putting toy food on a toy plate

movement_physical.text: Kicks a ball
Runs
Walks (not climbs) up a few stairs with or without help
Eats with a spoon

social_emotional.text: Plays next to other children and sometimes plays with them
Shows you what she can do by saying, "Look at me!"
Follows simple routines when told, like helping to pick up toys when you say, "It's clean-up time."

language_communication.text: Says about 50 words
Says two or more words together, with one action word, like "Doggie run"
Names things in a book when you point and ask, "What is this?"
Says words like "I," "me," or "we"

cognitive.text: Uses things to pretend, like feeding a block to a doll as if it were food
Shows simple problem-solving skills, like standing on a small stool to reach something
Follows two-step instructions like "Put the toy down and close the door."
Shows he knows at least one color, like pointing to a red crayon when you ask, "Which one is red?"

movement_physical.text: Uses hands to twist things, like turning doorknobs or unscrewing lids
Takes some clothes off by himself, like loose pants or an open jacket
Jumps off the ground with both feet
Turns book pages, one at a time, when you read to her

social_emotional.text: Calms down within 10 minutes after you leave her, like at a childcare drop off
Notices other children and joins them to play

language_communication.text: Talks with you in conversation using at least two back-and-forth exchanges
Asks "who," "what," "where," or "why" questions, like "Where is mommy/daddy?"
Says what action is happening in a picture or book when asked, like "running," "eating," or "playing"
Says first name, when asked
Talks well enough for others to understand, most of the time

cognitive.text: Draws a circle, when you show him how
Avoids touching hot objects, like a stove, when you warn her

movement_physical.text: Strings items together, like large beads or macaroni
Puts on some clothes by himself, like loose pants or a jacket
Uses a fork

social_emotional.text: Pretends to be something else during play (teacher, superhero, dog)
Asks to go play with children if none are around, like "Can I play with Alex?"
Comforts others who are hurt or sad, like hugging a crying friend
Avoids danger, like not jumping from tall heights at the playground
Likes to be a "helper"
Changes behavior based on where she is (place of worship, library, playground)

language_communication.text: Says sentences with four or more words
Says some words from a song, story, or nursery rhyme
Talks about at least one thing that happened during her day, like "I played soccer."
Answers simple questions like "What is a coat for?" or "What is a crayon for?"

cognitive.text: Names a few colors of items
Tells what comes next in a well-known story
Draws a person with three or more body parts

movement_physical.text: Catches a large ball most of the time
Serves herself food or pours water, with adult supervision
Unbuttons some buttons
Holds crayon or pencil between fingers and thumb (not a fist)

social_emotional.text: Follows rules or takes turns when playing games with other children
Sings, dances, or acts for you
Does simple chores at home, like matching socks or clearing the table after eating

language_communication.text: Tells a story she heard or made up with at least two events, for example, a cat was stuck in a tree and a firefighter saved it
Answers simple questions about a book or story after you read or tell it to him
Keeps a conversation going with more than three back-and-forth exchanges
Uses or recognizes simple rhymes (bat-cat, ball-tall)

cognitive.text: Counts to 10
Names some numbers between 1 and 5 when you point to them
Uses words about time, like "yesterday," "tomorrow," "morning," or "night"
Pays attention for 5 to 10 minutes during activities, for example, during story time or making arts and crafts (screen time does not count)
Writes some letters in her name
Names some letters when you point to them

movement_physical.text: Buttons some buttons
Hops on one foot
